survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 mathematics achievement and questionnaire variables to build classification models that predict students’ achievement-level group membership (6, 3, and 2 subgroups). The analytic sample is constructed by excluding students with missing values on the 17 selected predictors, and by further restricting to students at or above PISA Level 1 (i.e., excluding “Less than Level 1”). The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure; therefore, it is unclear whether complex survey design was accounted for in model estimation or evaluation. Because the models are trained in SPSS using standard ANN/CHAID/linear discriminant analysis workflows, analysts should treat the results as potentially unweighted and interpret performance as classification accuracy under the constructed samples rather than population-representative estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA 2012 mathematics test and survey data. The study defines achievement-level groups based on PISA 2012 mathematics achievement levels (Level 1–Level 6) and excludes students below Level 1 (“Less than Level 1”) when forming the 6-, 3-, and 2-subgroup classification targets. From the full PISA 2012 mathematics practice sample of 485,490 students across all participating countries, students with missing data in the 17 selected independent/predictive variables are excluded, leaving 126,126 students for the largest analytic sample. Additional subsamples are created for robustness to sample size: medium (6,186), small (603), and very small (102) samples, using systematic sampling after ranking students by achievement level; very small samples are also constructed under conditions where variance-covariance homogeneity is ensured vs not ensured.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; achievement levels mapped to 6 subgroups)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Classification accuracy (percentage). ANNs: best in large/medium/small; highest single-trial performance 55.0% in very small sample with variance-covariance homogeneity ensured; average best performance 39.9% in very small sample with homogeneity ensured. DTs (CHAID): highest in medium sample; peak 35.4% in medium; drops to 16.7% in very small sample with homogeneity not ensured. DA (linear discriminant): sensitive to homogeneity; performance increases as sample size decreases; reaches 66.7% in very small sample with homogeneity ensured; 54.9% when homogeneity not ensured.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged Math anxiety, Mathematics self-efficacy, Math motivation, Sense of belonging to school, and Teacher classroom management to predict achievement level membership into 6 subgroups, finding that ANNs achieved the highest overall classification performance in larger samples while DA performed best in very small samples when variance-covariance homogeneity was ensured. This indicates that the choice of classification method should depend on the available sample size and distributional assumptions, with neural networks being preferable for typical sample sizes and discriminant analysis potentially outperforming only under very small, assumption-satisfying conditions.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; achievement levels mapped to 3 subgroups)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Classification accuracy (percentage). ANNs: best in large/medium/small; average best performance 63.1% in small; highest single-trial performance 74.2% in very small sample with homogeneity ensured. DTs (CHAID): highest 59.5% in medium; drops to 33.3% in very small sample with homogeneity not ensured. DA (linear discriminant): highest 74.5% in very small sample with homogeneity ensured; 57.8% when homogeneity not ensured; performance increases as sample size decreases.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged Math anxiety, Mathematics self-efficacy, Math motivation, Mathematics interest, and Teacher-student relations to predict achievement level membership into 3 subgroups, finding that ANNs were most successful across larger samples while DA and ANNs both reached their top performances in very small samples when variance-covariance homogeneity was ensured. This indicates that for practical educational classification tasks with moderate-to-large datasets, neural networks are likely to provide more stable accuracy, whereas discriminant analysis can be competitive only when sample size is extremely small and its assumptions are met.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds; achievement levels mapped to 2 subgroups)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Classification accuracy (percentage). ANNs: best in large/medium/small; average best performance 78.2% in large; highest single-trial performance 89.0% in very small sample with homogeneity not ensured; average in very small with homogeneity ensured 82.1%. DTs (CHAID): highest 76.9% in medium; drops to 50.0% in very small sample with homogeneity not ensured. DA (linear discriminant): highest 82.4% in small sample with homogeneity ensured; 75.5% in very small sample with homogeneity not ensured; performance increases as sample size decreases.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study leveraged Math anxiety, Mathematics self-efficacy, Math motivation, Openness to problem solving, and Math teacher support to predict achievement level membership into 2 subgroups, finding that ANNs achieved the highest overall performance in larger samples and also reached the top single-trial accuracy in very small samples even when homogeneity was not ensured. This indicates that neural networks are a strong default for binary achievement classification using student and school/teacher factors, while discriminant analysis and decision trees may be more sensitive to sample size and variance-covariance homogeneity conditions.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2012 mathematics test and questionnaire data to compare three classification approaches—multilayer perceptron neural networks, CHAID decision trees, and linear discriminant analysis—under varying target granularities (6, 3, and 2 achievement subgroups) and constructed sample sizes (126,126; 6,186; 603; 102). Students below PISA Level 1 are excluded and cases with missing values on 17 selected predictors are removed, yielding an analytic sample of 126,126. For the 6- and 3-subgroup tasks, neural networks are reported as the most successful method in large/medium/small samples, while discriminant analysis can outperform in very small samples when variance-covariance homogeneity is ensured. For the 2-subgroup task, neural networks again lead in larger samples, with the highest single-trial accuracy reported as 89.0% in a very small sample. The paper does not report PISA sampling-weight usage, and performance is based on constructed subsamples and repeated ANN train/test splits, so results should be interpreted as methodological comparisons rather than population-representative effects.
